reading.title: Naming Big Feelings
reading.purpose: Learn how exact words help you describe strong feelings to others.
paras: Everyone has feelings that change from hour to hour. Some feelings are small, like feeling a little glad or a bit tired. Other feelings are much bigger, and exact words help you share them clearly.

Think about happy and surprised feelings. When you get great news, you may feel delighted, which means very happy and pleased. If a friend pulls off a trick you did not expect, you might feel astonished, as if you can hardly believe what you saw.

Hard feelings also come in different sizes. Before a big play or a test, you may feel anxious, worried and nervous about what could go wrong. If a noisy room has too many jobs at once, you can feel overwhelmed. When a math step makes no sense, you might be puzzled, or even bewildered, so confused that you feel lost.

Strong upset feelings need careful words too. You might feel furious when something seems deeply unfair and you want to shout. A sudden loud crash in the dark can leave someone terrified, so scared that they freeze in place. After a long hike in cold rain, a wet hiker can feel miserable and exhausted, with no energy left at all.
Naming a feeling does not make it vanish, yet it helps you ask for what you need.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "bewildered" most nearly means
choices: angry about a rule that seems completely unfair
so confused that you feel lost
happy and pleased about some wonderful news
tired after walking a long way in the rain
qs.why: The sentence explains it directly: bewildered means "so confused that you feel lost."

qs.q: Which sentence tells what might make a person feel terrified?
choices: Strong upset feelings need careful words too.
You might feel furious when something seems deeply unfair and you want to shout.
A sudden loud crash in the dark can leave someone terrified, so scared that they freeze in place.
Naming a feeling does not make it vanish, yet it helps you ask for what you need.
qs.why: This sentence names a sudden loud crash in the dark as something that can leave someone terrified.

ev.text: A sudden loud crash in the dark can leave someone terrified, so scared that they freeze in place.

qs.q: Sam has three chores, a barking dog, and a ringing phone all at the same time. Which word from the reading fits how Sam feels?
qs.why: The reading explains that having too many jobs at once in a noisy room can make you feel overwhelmed.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Hiking in cold rain is the fastest way to lose all of your energy outdoors.
People should only talk about happy feelings and hide any hard feelings.
Exact feeling words help people name strong emotions and ask for help.
Math problems and school plays always make students feel nervous or lost.
qs.why: The passage introduces exact words for different strong feelings and ends by explaining that naming them helps you ask for what you need.
